fetched_contents.text: Physiotherapy assessment for female urinary incontinence Abstract Introduction and hypothesis As noted in the 6th International Consultation on Incontinence (ICI) chapter “Initial Management of Urinary Incontinence in Women” recommendations call for including physiotherapy as a first-line therapy. Methods Building on this, checking available scientific evidence and using the International Classification of Functioning, Disabilities and Health, the following represents a holistic physiotherapist approach for initial evaluation of the health problem of urinary incontinence. Results This paper proposes a teaching module for every relevant health care professional dealing with the assessment of adult female urinary incontinence, focusing on optimal patient selection and appropriate treatment choice. Conclusion The assessment stage involves the explicit decision as to whether “physiotherapy” is the treatment indicated for the patient, based on the findings of the physiotherapy assessment and supplemented by any medical information that accompanied the referral and evaluation. Keywords: Female, Urinary incontinence, Assessment, (Pelvic) Physiotherapy, Diagnostic, Initial management, Psychometric measurement Introduction In this paper the main focus is on physiotherapy. However, it is intended as a proposal and starting point to discuss and develop a teaching module for every relevant health care professional dealing with the assessment and treatment of female urinary incontinence (UI). As noted in the 6th International Consultation on Incontinence (ICI), recommendations for the initial management of adult female UI are based on a medical diagnosis that does not always take into account co-morbidities or functional limitations that can affect outcomes [1]. This means that sometimes a patient with unclear and/or underlying pathology that is not amendable to physical therapy is referred to physiotherapy for treatment. Without taking these issues into consideration, therapy is often disappointing and has inadequate results. A holistic structured and systematic physiotherapy assessment in women with UI may help to improve patient selection and identify those who will benefit most from physiotherapy. Materials and methods Two out of the three authors of this paper (BB, ATMB) were originators of the evidence-based Royal Dutch Society for Physiotherapy (KNGF) guidelines for UI, which have been developed, implemented and published in multiple languages [2]. These guidelines have been extensively checked with relevant literature and available national and international guidelines [2]. For this paper we again performed a systematic literature search (see Appendixes 1, 2) between 1998 and November 2019 in the following databases: PUBMED, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PEDro, and the Cochrane database. Publications about the methods of diagnosing stress, urgency, and mixed UI and about their reliability, validity, and feasibility of assessment for physiotherapy in routine practice, were retrieved. According to this, the grade of recommendation in the area of “initial assessment,” which is mostly the case in conservative management, has little evidence outside of “expert opinion,” which is a recognized limitation (Level 4, Grade D) [3]. fetched_contents.text: Accuracy and Reliability of Different Approaches for the Assessment of Pelvic Floor Muscle Strength: A Systematic Review ABSTRACT There had been various methods employed for the evaluation of pelvic floor muscle (PFM) strength. The aim of the study was to do a systemic review of these methods for a better understanding of these techniques and to find the best appropriate method. A systemic review of the literature was done using three databases that included: PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science using the keywords “pelvic floor anatomy” and “functional anatomy of pelvic floor muscles” from 1985 to 2022. All the studies involved were analyzed for the methodologies used by the researcher, advantages, disadvantages, and the conclusion of the study. A total of 1,876 studies were found, out of which only 64 met the criteria of inclusion. In these studies, seven methods were used for the determination of PFM strength. These methods included: clinical palpation, perineometer, electromyography, dynamometer, ultrasonography, magnetic resonance imaging, and vaginal cones. The PFM cannot be calculated accurately using any one measuring technique. There is therefore no “gold standard” approach to PFM assessment. However, combining these methods will result in the best outcomes. According to the literature review, the most often employed procedures were digital palpation, perineometry, and Ultrasonography (USG). KEYWORDS: Assessment, muscle strength, pelvic floor, perineometer INTRODUCTION The pelvic floor performs a variety of vital tasks, including holding our organs in place, preventing leakage, and even enhancing the quality and function of sexual activity. By fully promoting the pelvic organs and covering the pelvic apertures with their anterior and cephalad action during contraction, the pelvic floor muscle (PFM), which makes up the pelvic basin’s floor, aids in sustaining continence.[1] The PFM typically undergoes synchronous mass contractions. A rise toward the inside and compression around the pelvic apertures has been defined as the proper PFM motion.[2] The diaphragmatic shape of the PFM muscle and its attachments to the endopelvic fascia and pelvic organs make it difficult to measure the muscle’s action. The evaluation of PFM strength is a crucial part of the clinical and technical discourse on pelvic floor training.[3] A technique for measuring PFM strength must be both objective and universal in order to give the precise baseline and endpoint measurements needed for optimal exercise prescription and successful treatment of PFM dysfunction. In order to measure PFM strength in females, this research will give a comprehensive evaluation of clinical techniques that are currently accessible. The accuracy of current techniques, their use, their drawbacks, and potential future possibilities for assessing PFM strength will all be covered in this study. REVIEW Search strategy and selection criteria To check the liabilities of the methods used for the analysis of PFM strength, a comprehensive literature search was conducted in the indexes of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science using the title search phrases including functions and anatomy of pelvic floor, that were associated with skeletal muscle strength measurement. In order to obtain entire papers that were not accessible via internet resources, a medical librarian was used. The following criteria were followed for inclusion of the articles: all the articles that were using PFM testing modalities, papers dealing with PFM anatomy and dysfunctions, and the studies analyzing the association between different methods of PFM strength measurement. The literature not available in English language was excluded. Study selection All the articles that were included were reviewed by 2 different reviewers at different time, and if any conflict occurred between the two another reviewer was also involved to comment on the included literature. All the papers included were tested for their eligibility by the reviewers. Figure 1 is depicting the format followed for including the studies. A total of 1,876 articles were searched, out of which only 64 met the inclusion criteria for the systemic review. Forty-nine articles were available in full text and for the rest fifteen a medical librarian was contacted to retrieve the article. fetched_contents.text: Physical Therapy Guide to Urinary Incontinence Urinary incontinence (bladder control problems) is any leakage of urine that can occur during the day or night. More than 13 million people in the United States have urinary incontinence. Physical therapists design treatment programs to improve help people gain control over the condition. They also help people reduce their need for medicines and surgery. Physical therapists are movement experts. They improve quality of life through hands-on care, patient education, and prescribed movement. You can contact a physical therapist directly for an evaluation. To find a physical therapist in your area, visit Find a PT. Find a PT Near You! What Is Urinary Incontinence? Urinary incontinence is any undesired leakage of urine. A person with the condition also may have trouble starting the urine stream or holding urine. Urinary incontinence involves the muscles of the pelvic floor. These muscles attach to the bottom of the pelvic bones. They run from front to back and create the base of your core (torso, between the pelvic floor and diaphragm). They form a hammock structure that lifts and supports the internal organs. The pelvic floor muscles also: * Control the sphincter muscles (ringlike muscles that open and close certain body openings). * Support the low back. * Stabilize the pelvic bones. * Help with sexual function. Women may be more likely than men to have urinary incontinence. However, men may under-report the condition. Different types of urinary incontinence include: Stress incontinence. Leakage happens when movement or physical activity puts excess pressure on the bladder. Leakage may occur because the pelvic floor muscles are weak and lack control. Leakage due to stress incontinence often occurs during: * Coughing, laughing, or sneezing. * Physical activities such as running. * Heavy lifting. Urge incontinence. This is a sudden, strong need to pass urine. People with this type of incontinence often experience a leak before reaching the bathroom. Mixed incontinence. Some people experience both stress and urge incontinence. Functional incontinence. This type of incontinence results from problems other than weak pelvic floor muscles or Urinary frequency. Some people feel the need to empty their bladder frequently throughout the day. They also need to go to the bathroom more than once during the night. It may be caused by infection or other conditions that affect the urinary tract (kidneys, bladder, and the tubes or ducts through which urine flows). Stress Incontinence The pelvic floor muscles and urogenital diaphragm (fibrous and muscle structures below the diaphragm) surround the urethra (the tube through which urine leaves the body). They help keep it closed when pressure is placed on the bladder. Stress incontinence occurs when these structures are weak or fail to support the urethra. It can occur with: * Laughing, sneezing, or coughing. * Activities such as lifting. Muscle strength assessment methods and typical measurements

Pelvic floor muscle strength assessment should be treated as a combination of objective and subjective methods because no single method is universally considered the “gold standard.” The evidence review explicitly states that multiple methods have been used, including clinical palpation, perineometer, electromyography, dynamometer, ultrasonography, magnetic resonance imaging, and vaginal cones, and that no one method can accurately calculate PFM strength alone [N2-F2]. A practical implication is that therapists should use the most clinically feasible method for the patient, with perineometry and ultrasonography highlighted as among the most commonly used methods in the literature [N2-F2].

For measurement, the review also emphasizes reproducibility and reliability. It notes that the evaluation of PFM strength is a crucial part of clinical and technical discourse, and that a technique must be both objective and universal to provide precise baseline and endpoint measurements [N2-F2]. This means assessments should be standardized across sessions and practitioners where possible. The review also identifies digital palpation and perineometry as among the most often employed procedures [N2-F2], which is useful for documentation because it means therapists can record whether the chosen method is palpation, perineometry, or another objective test.

### What measurements are typically recorded?

The evidence base suggests that assessment should cover contraction, endurance, and coordination. The PERFECT acronym in the search result provides a useful framework: P = power (pressure, a measure of strength using a manometric perineometer), E = endurance, R = repetitions, F = fast [N2-R2]. This indicates that therapists should routinely record strength under load or pressure, how long the muscle can sustain contraction, and the number or quality of repeated contractions. A separate source also notes that clinicians may use a modified Oxford scale in combination with vaginal palpation [N2-R5], which can be used to rate perceived strength on a scale from 1 to 5 or similar.

In practice, a standard record should therefore include:
- Baseline contraction strength: e.g., pressure reading or Oxford-scale score [N2-R2][N2-R5]
- Endurance: how many sustained contractions can be performed in sequence [N2-R2]
- Coordination: whether contractions are smooth, symmetrical, and appropriate [N2-F2][N2-R2]
- Any signs of weakness, tightness, or abnormal muscle behavior [N2-F2]

### How to interpret results in relation to clinical relevance and treatment planning

Interpretation should be tied to whether the findings support a diagnosis of pelvic floor dysfunction and guide treatment. The evidence review notes that PFM strength assessment is part of the clinical discourse on pelvic floor training and is essential for exercise prescription and successful treatment [N2-F2]. It also states that clinical palpation and perineometry are the most commonly used procedures, which implies that therapists should interpret these findings in the context of the patient’s symptoms and response to therapy [N2-F2].

In treatment planning, weak contraction or poor endurance suggests the need for strengthening exercises, while coordination problems or tightness may point to neuromuscular retraining or biofeedback [N2-F2][N2-R2]. The evidence from postpartum rehabilitation also supports the use of evidence-based treatment plans rooted in current research on postpartum pelvic floor rehab [N5-R4], which reinforces that assessment findings should directly inform the plan rather than be treated as standalone numbers.

### Reproducibility and interpretation caveats

The literature review explicitly cautions that no one method can accurately calculate PFM strength, and that combining methods tends to produce the best outcomes [N2-F2]. This means therapists should document whether multiple methods were used, which method was chosen, and whether findings were consistent across methods. The review also notes that correlation studies have shown variable agreement between digital palpation and perineometry, with some studies reporting moderate to significant correlation and others weaker correlation [N2-F2]. Therefore, interpretation should include a note on method limitations and whether results are within expected ranges for the patient’s condition.

Overall, the recommended documentation for muscle strength assessment should include the method used, contraction strength, endurance, coordination, any abnormal findings, and a clinical interpretation linking these to treatment goals [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R5].

Frequency and plan of care recommendations

The evidence base supports a structured, evidence-based care plan for postpartum urinary incontinence, with reassessment and modification based on response to therapy. The APTA pelvic health guide states that physical therapists design treatment programs to improve pelvic floor muscle strength and help people gain control over the condition, and that treatment plans should be customized [N3-F3]. It also notes that physical therapists may refer patients to a doctor for urodynamic testing or other investigations if needed, which is useful for planning reassessment [N3-F3]. The postpartum pelvic floor therapy source adds that many moms start therapy within six weeks after delivery, but care is never too late, which supports a flexible but timely reassessment schedule [N5-R2].

### How often to reassess muscle strength and symptoms during therapy

The evidence does not provide a single fixed interval for reassessment, but the APTA guide emphasizes that the treatment program is tailored and that the physical therapist will perform a thorough exam and may refer for additional tests [N3-F3]. The physiotherapy assessment paper also notes that the assessment process is used to optimize patient selection and formulate a specific treatment plan, implying that reassessment should occur at intervals sufficient to monitor response and adjust the plan [N1-F1]. In practice, the most defensible approach is to reassess muscle strength and symptoms at regular intervals, such as 4–6 weeks after the initial evaluation, and then more frequently if the patient is responding poorly or if new symptoms emerge [N3-F3][N5-R2].

The physiotherapy assessment source also mentions severity calculation based on frequency counts for each response, which suggests that symptom frequency and severity should be tracked over time rather than assessed only once [N4-R5]. This supports the idea of using a diary or symptom tracker as part of the care plan [N1-F1][N4-R5].

### When to advance or modify the plan of care based on response

The evidence supports advancing or modifying the plan when there is a clear response to therapy. The postpartum pelvic floor therapy source states that treatment plans are designed to reduce or eliminate PFD symptoms and long-term complications, and that therapy can help patients feel strong and confident [N5-R3]. The APTA guide similarly states that the goal is to improve pelvic floor muscle function and reduce the need for pads, special underwear, and medicine [N3-F3]. If the patient shows improvement in contraction strength, endurance, coordination, and symptom frequency, the plan should be advanced; if there is little change or worsening, the plan should be modified [N3-F3][N5-R3].

The physiotherapy assessment paper also emphasizes that the assessment stage includes explicit decision-making about whether physiotherapy is indicated and what the treatment plan should be [N1-F1]. This implies that reassessment should trigger a decision point: if the patient is improving, advance the plan; if not, consider changing the intervention or investigating other causes [N1-F1][N3-F3].

### What evidence-based components should be included in the plan of care

A strong evidence-based plan should include the following components:
1. **Muscle-strengthening exercises**: the evidence supports strengthening the pelvic floor and improving awareness and movement [N3-F3].
2. **Biofeedback or manual facilitation**: although not explicitly detailed in the provided evidence, the assessment framework in the physiotherapy paper implies that objective assessment informs whether biofeedback or manual techniques are needed [N1-F1][N2-F2].
3. **Pelvic floor retraining**: the evidence base supports improving coordination and control [N3-F3].
4. **Education and lifestyle counseling**: the APTA guide states that physical therapists improve quality of life through patient education and prescribed movement, and the postpartum source mentions trauma-informed care and clear communication [N3-F3][N5-R4].
5. **Referral for investigations**: when the physical therapist identifies red flags or unclear pathology, referral for urodynamic testing or other investigations is appropriate [N3-F3][N1-F1].
6. **Progress monitoring**: tracking symptoms, frequency, and strength over time [N4-R5][N1-F1].

In short, the plan should be evidence-based, patient-centered, and dynamic: it should be reassessed regularly, advanced when the patient improves, and modified when the response is inadequate [N3-F3][N5-R2][N1-F1].

- **Impairment**: structural, physiological, or anatomical issues related to the pelvic floor or urinary system [N1-F1].

- Type of examination method used
- Contraction strength and pressure or Oxford-scale score
- Endurance and repetition capacity
- Coordination and movement pattern
- Any signs of tightness, weakness, or pain

Differential diagnosis and clinical decision-making framework

The evidence supports a structured differential diagnosis approach for postpartum urinary incontinence, distinguishing pelvic floor dysfunction from other pelvic and non-pelvic causes. The physiotherapy assessment paper explicitly states that the initial management of urinary incontinence should be based on a medical diagnosis that may not always account for co-morbidities or functional limitations [N1-F1]. This means the therapist must consider both pelvic floor-related and non-pelvic contributors before deciding on physiotherapy as the primary intervention.

### How to distinguish postpartum urinary incontinence from other pelvic floor and non-pelvic causes

The evidence base suggests that postpartum urinary incontinence is often attributed to pelvic floor dysfunction, but it may also be caused by other pelvic structures or non-pelvic conditions. The APTA guide explains that urinary incontinence involves the muscles of the pelvic floor, but also notes that different types of incontinence may have different underlying mechanisms, including stress incontinence, urge incontinence, mixed incontinence, and functional incontinence [N3-F3]. The physiotherapy assessment paper similarly emphasizes that the assessment process investigates the nature of the underlying disorders and co-existing functional limitations [N1-F1].

Key differentiating features include:
- **Stress incontinence**: leakage with physical activity, coughing, laughing, or lifting; often linked to pelvic floor weakness or trauma [N3-F3].
- **Urge incontinence**: sudden, strong need to void with possible leakage before reaching the toilet; may reflect detrusor overactivity or poor coordination [N3-F3].
- **Mixed incontinence**: combination of stress and urge symptoms [N3-F3].
- **Functional incontinence**: caused by mobility, cognition, depression, or barriers to access, not directly by pelvic floor weakness [N3-F3].
- **Non-pelvic causes**: conditions such as infection, bladder outlet obstruction, diabetes, Parkinson disease, or neurological disorders [N6-R1][N6-R2].

The evidence also notes that the pelvic floor examination can help identify functional limitations and co-morbidities that affect outcomes [N1-F1]. This means the therapist should ask about fatigue, pain, mobility, cognition, and other factors that may limit participation or explain persistent symptoms [N1-F1][N3-F3].

### When to refer for urodynamic testing or other investigations

The evidence supports referral when the clinical picture is unclear or when the therapist identifies red flags. The physiotherapy assessment paper states that before starting the physiotherapy assessing process, the therapist should screen for pathological conditions that would require medical consultation and pay particular attention to red flags [N1-F1]. The APTA guide also notes that the physical therapist may refer the patient to a doctor for more tests, including urodynamic testing or imaging [N3-F3].

Urodynamic testing is explicitly described in the physiotherapy assessment paper as a gold standard for condition-specific diagnosis, though it is typically done in secondary care [N1-R2]. This makes it a useful investigation when the therapist is uncertain about the diagnosis, the patient has failed conservative management, or there are atypical symptoms such as unexplained leakage, frequent urination, or pain [N1-F1][N1-R2].

Other investigations may include:
- Pelvic examination to assess for atrophic vaginitis or vulvar irritation [N6-R2][N6-R3]
- Urinalysis or culture for infection [N6-R1]
- Imaging or MRI if structural abnormalities are suspected [N1-R2]

### How to document findings that support or refute a specific diagnosis

Documentation should clearly link findings to diagnostic possibilities. The evidence-based assessment framework recommends using the ICF model to distinguish impairment, disability, and participation restriction [N1-F1]. This means the therapist should document:
- Whether the patient’s symptoms are consistent with stress, urge, mixed, or functional incontinence
- Whether pelvic floor findings support weak contraction, poor endurance, or coordination
- Whether there are signs of tightness, pain, or abnormal movement that point to a different diagnosis
- Whether co-morbidities or functional limitations are present and may explain the symptoms [N1-F1][N3-F3]

The differential diagnosis aid (DIAPPERS) is useful for organizing reversible causes, including delirium, infection, constipation, medication use, pain, endocrine disease, and structural obstruction [N6-R1]. This can be used to document which reversible factors have been ruled in or out and what remains to be investigated [N6-R1].

In summary, the clinical decision-making framework should be evidence-based and patient-centered: start with a thorough history and examination, use a structured differential diagnosis, and refer for urodynamic or other investigations when the clinical picture is unclear or when red flags are present [N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

A standardized initial evaluation template should be structured to capture patient history, symptoms, functional impact, pelvic floor examination findings, and differential considerations. The evidence from the physiotherapy assessment paper is particularly relevant because it proposes a holistic physiotherapist approach for the initial evaluation of urinary incontinence, focusing on optimal patient selection and appropriate treatment choice [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that the assessment stage includes explicit decision-making about whether physiotherapy is indicated and what the treatment plan should be [N1-F1]. This means the template should be organized around a clear flow from patient information to diagnosis to treatment planning.

### What sections should appear in a standard initial evaluation template

Based on the provided evidence, a standard template should include the following sections:
1. **Patient identification and referral information**: name, date of birth, date of assessment, referral source, and any accompanying medical information [N1-F1].
2. **Chief complaint and reason for referral**: the patient’s main concern and why they sought physiotherapy [N1-F1].
3. **History of present illness and urinary symptoms**: onset, duration, frequency, urgency, leakage pattern, triggers, and any associated symptoms [N1-F1][N3-F3].
4. **Medical and obstetric history**: previous pregnancies, deliveries, episiotomy, perineal trauma, surgeries, infections, and other relevant medical history [N3-F3].
5. **Medications and supplements**: because these can affect pelvic floor function and treatment [N1-F1].
6. **Concurrent symptoms and functional limitations**: pain, sexual function, bowel function, core stability, and mobility [N1-F1][N3-F3].
7. **Pelvic floor examination findings**: contraction, endurance, coordination, strength, tightness, pain, and any abnormal movement [N1-F1][N2-F2].
8. **Differential diagnosis and red flags**: which symptoms or findings suggest other causes and require further investigation [N1-F1][N6-R1].
9. **Assessment of patient readiness for therapy**: whether the patient is a good candidate for physiotherapy and whether further medical evaluation is indicated [N1-F1].
10. **Plan of care and next steps**: proposed treatment, frequency of reassessment, and referrals [N1-F1][N3-F3].

### How to organize patient history, symptoms, and functional impact

The evidence supports a chronological and functional organization of the patient’s history. The physiotherapy assessment paper notes that the assessment process investigates the nature of the underlying disorders and co-existing functional limitations that affect urinary incontinence [N1-F1]. It also uses the ICF framework, which separates impairment, disability, and participation restrictions [N1-F1]. This means the history should be organized around:
- **Impairment**: structural, physiological, or anatomical issues related to the pelvic floor or urinary system [N1-F1].
- **Disability**: restriction or loss of ability to perform normal functions or activities [N1-F1].
- **Participation restrictions**: how the condition limits the patient’s role, mobility, or daily activities [N1-F1].

For symptoms, the template should capture not only the type and frequency of urinary leakage but also the context in which it occurs, such as stress, urgency, or functional incontinence [N3-F3]. The APTA guide also notes that physical therapists assess the muscles of the pelvis, hips, and lower back, coordination, strength, and flexibility, which supports including musculoskeletal and core-related symptoms in the history [N3-F3].

### How to include pelvic floor examination findings and differential considerations

The pelvic floor examination should be documented objectively and clinically. The evidence review indicates that digital palpation and perineometry are among the most commonly used procedures, and that objective assessment is important for accurate baseline and endpoint measurements [N2-F2]. The PERFECT scheme also provides a useful framework for documenting contraction, endurance, repetitions, and fast movement [N2-R2]. The assessment template should therefore include:
- Type of examination method used
- Contraction strength and pressure or Oxford-scale score
- Endurance and repetition capacity
- Coordination and movement pattern
- Any signs of tightness, weakness, or pain
- Any abnormal findings such as asymmetry, spasm, or lack of control [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R5]

For differential considerations, the evidence supports using a structured approach. The physiotherapy assessment paper emphasizes red flags that may indicate a need for medical consultation, such as unexplained incontinence or other worrisome symptoms [N1-F1]. The StatPearls differential diagnosis aid also provides a mnemonic (DIAPPERS) for reversible causes of urinary incontinence, which can help organize differential thinking [N6-R1]. The NHS and AAFP sources also note that a pelvic examination is part of the diagnostic process, and that external gynecologic examination can detect atrophic vaginitis or vulvar irritation [N6-R2][N6-R3].

In practice, the template should document:
- Which symptoms or findings support a pelvic floor diagnosis
- Which findings raise concern for non-pelvic or other pelvic causes
- Whether further investigations are indicated [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3]

Overall, the template should be concise but comprehensive, with sections that mirror the evidence-based assessment process: patient identification, symptoms, history, examination findings, differential considerations, and treatment planning [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Differential diagnosis and clinical decision-making framework

The evidence supports a structured differential diagnosis approach for postpartum urinary incontinence, distinguishing pelvic floor dysfunction from other pelvic and non-pelvic causes. The physiotherapy assessment paper explicitly states that the initial management of urinary incontinence should be based on a medical diagnosis that may not always account for co-morbidities or functional limitations [N1-F1]. This means the therapist must consider both pelvic floor-related and non-pelvic contributors before deciding on physiotherapy as the primary intervention.

### How to distinguish postpartum urinary incontinence from other pelvic floor and non-pelvic causes

The evidence base suggests that postpartum urinary incontinence is often attributed to pelvic floor dysfunction, but it may also be caused by other pelvic structures or non-pelvic conditions. The APTA guide explains that urinary incontinence involves the muscles of the pelvic floor, but also notes that different types of incontinence may have different underlying mechanisms, including stress incontinence, urge incontinence, mixed incontinence, and functional incontinence [N3-F3]. The physiotherapy assessment paper similarly emphasizes that the assessment process investigates the nature of the underlying disorders and co-existing functional limitations [N1-F1].

Key differentiating features include:
- **Stress incontinence**: leakage with physical activity, coughing, laughing, or lifting; often linked to pelvic floor weakness or trauma [N3-F3].
- **Urge incontinence**: sudden, strong need to void with possible leakage before reaching the toilet; may reflect detrusor overactivity or poor coordination [N3-F3].
- **Mixed incontinence**: combination of stress and urge symptoms [N3-F3].
- **Functional incontinence**: caused by mobility, cognition, depression, or barriers to access, not directly by pelvic floor weakness [N3-F3].
- **Non-pelvic causes**: conditions such as infection, bladder outlet obstruction, diabetes, Parkinson disease, or neurological disorders [N6-R1][N6-R2].

The evidence also notes that the pelvic floor examination can help identify functional limitations and co-morbidities that affect outcomes [N1-F1]. This means the therapist should ask about fatigue, pain, mobility, cognition, and other factors that may limit participation or explain persistent symptoms [N1-F1][N3-F3].

### When to refer for urodynamic testing or other investigations

The evidence supports referral when the clinical picture is unclear or when the therapist identifies red flags. The physiotherapy assessment paper states that before starting the physiotherapy assessing process, the therapist should screen for pathological conditions that would require medical consultation and pay particular attention to red flags [N1-F1]. The APTA guide also notes that the physical therapist may refer the patient to a doctor for more tests, including urodynamic testing or imaging [N3-F3].

Urodynamic testing is explicitly described in the physiotherapy assessment paper as a gold standard for condition-specific diagnosis, though it is typically done in secondary care [N1-R2]. This makes it a useful investigation when the therapist is uncertain about the diagnosis, the patient has failed conservative management, or there are atypical symptoms such as unexplained leakage, frequent urination, or pain [N1-F1][N1-R2].

Other investigations may include:
- Pelvic examination to assess for atrophic vaginitis or vulvar irritation [N6-R2][N6-R3]
- Urinalysis or culture for infection [N6-R1]
- Imaging or MRI if structural abnormalities are suspected [N1-R2]

### How to document findings that support or refute a specific diagnosis

Documentation should clearly link findings to diagnostic possibilities. The evidence-based assessment framework recommends using the ICF model to distinguish impairment, disability, and participation restriction [N1-F1]. This means the therapist should document:
- Whether the patient’s symptoms are consistent with stress, urge, mixed, or functional incontinence
- Whether pelvic floor findings support weak contraction, poor endurance, or coordination
- Whether there are signs of tightness, pain, or abnormal movement that point to a different diagnosis
- Whether co-morbidities or functional limitations are present and may explain the symptoms [N1-F1][N3-F3]

The differential diagnosis aid (DIAPPERS) is useful for organizing reversible causes, including delirium, infection, constipation, medication use, pain, endocrine disease, and structural obstruction [N6-R1]. This can be used to document which reversible factors have been ruled in or out and what remains to be investigated [N6-R1].

In summary, the clinical decision-making framework should be evidence-based and patient-centered: start with a thorough history and examination, use a structured differential diagnosis, and refer for urodynamic or other investigations when the clinical picture is unclear or when red flags are present [N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

## 2. Recommended muscle strength assessment methods and typical measurements

Pelvic floor muscle strength assessment should be treated as a combination of objective and subjective methods because no single method is universally considered the “gold standard.” The evidence review explicitly states that multiple methods have been used, including clinical palpation, perineometer, electromyography, dynamometer, ultrasonography, magnetic resonance imaging, and vaginal cones, and that no one method can accurately calculate PFM strength alone [N2-F2]. ### How to measure pelvic floor muscle strength

The evidence supports a structured measurement process that includes reproducibility and interpretation. The review notes that PFM strength assessment is a crucial part of clinical and technical discourse, and that a technique must be both objective and universal to provide precise baseline and endpoint measurements [N2-F2]. This means assessments should be standardized across sessions and practitioners where possible. ### What measurements are typically recorded

The evidence base suggests that assessment should cover contraction, endurance, and coordination. The PERFECT acronym in the search result provides a useful framework: P = power (pressure, a measure of strength using a manometric perineometer), E = endurance, R = repetitions, F = fast [N2-R2]. This indicates that therapists should routinely record strength under load or pressure, how long the muscle can sustain contraction, and the number or quality of repeated contractions. A separate source also notes that clinicians may use a modified Oxford scale in combination with vaginal palpation [N2-R5], which can be used to rate perceived strength on a scale from 1 to 5 or similar.

In practice, a standard record should therefore include:
- **Baseline contraction strength**: e.g., pressure reading or Oxford-scale score [N2-R2][N2-R5]
- **Endurance**: how many sustained contractions can be performed in sequence [N2-R2]
- **Coordination**: whether contractions are smooth, symmetrical, and appropriate [N2-F2][N2-R2]
- Any signs of weakness, tightness, or abnormal muscle behavior [N2-F2]

Interpretation should be tied to whether the findings support a diagnosis of pelvic floor dysfunction and guide treatment. The evidence review notes that PFM strength assessment is part of the clinical discourse on pelvic floor training and is essential for exercise prescription and successful treatment [N2-F2]. It also states that clinical palpation and perineometry are the most commonly used procedures, which implies that therapists should interpret these findings in the context of the patient’s symptoms and response to therapy [N2-F2].

The evidence supports a structured differential diagnosis approach for postpartum urinary incontinence, distinguishing pelvic floor dysfunction from other pelvic and non-pelvic causes. The physiotherapy assessment paper explicitly states that the initial management of urinary incontinence should be based on a medical diagnosis that may not always account for co-morbidities or functional limitations [N1-F1]. This means the therapist must consider both pelvic floor-related and non-pelvic contributors before deciding on physiotherapy as the primary intervention.

### How to distinguish postpartum urinary incontinence from other pelvic floor and non-pelvic causes

The evidence base suggests that postpartum urinary incontinence is often attributed to pelvic floor dysfunction, but it may also be caused by other pelvic structures or non-pelvic conditions. The APTA guide explains that urinary incontinence involves the muscles of the pelvic floor, but also notes that different types of incontinence may have different underlying mechanisms, including stress incontinence, urge incontinence, mixed incontinence, and functional incontinence [N3-F3]. The physiotherapy assessment paper similarly emphasizes that the assessment process investigates the nature of the underlying disorders and co-existing functional limitations [N1-F1].

Key differentiating features include:
- **Stress incontinence**: leakage with physical activity, coughing, laughing, or lifting; often linked to pelvic floor weakness or trauma [N3-F3].
- **Urge incontinence**: sudden, strong need to void with possible leakage before reaching the toilet; may reflect detrusor overactivity or poor coordination [N3-F3].
- **Mixed incontinence**: combination of stress and urge symptoms [N3-F3].
- **Functional incontinence**: caused by mobility, cognition, depression, or barriers to access, not directly by pelvic floor weakness [N3-F3].
- **Non-pelvic causes**: conditions such as infection, bladder outlet obstruction, diabetes, Parkinson disease, or neurological disorders [N6-R1][N6-R2].

## Integrated final answer: recommended standardized template and evidence-based care plan for postpartum urinary incontinence

As a pelvic floor physical therapist, you need a standardized initial evaluation template that is both clinically comprehensive and evidence-based. The branch reports together support a structured template, objective muscle strength assessment methods, regular reassessment intervals, and a clear care plan informed by pelvic floor rehabilitation protocols and differential diagnosis. I’ve organized the answer into four sections: **template structure**, **muscle strength assessment**, **frequency and plan of care**, and **differential diagnosis**.

---

## 1. Recommended standardized template structure

A standard initial evaluation template for postpartum urinary incontinence should be organized around patient identification, history, symptoms, functional impact, pelvic floor examination findings, and differential considerations. The physiotherapy assessment paper explicitly proposes a holistic physiotherapist approach for the initial evaluation of urinary incontinence, emphasizing optimal patient selection and appropriate treatment choice [N1-F1]. It also states that the assessment stage includes explicit decision-making about whether physiotherapy is indicated and what the treatment plan should be [N1-F1].

### Sections to include in the template

1. **Patient identification and referral information**  
   - Name, date of birth, date of assessment, referral source, and any accompanying medical information [N1-F1].

2. **Chief complaint and reason for referral**  
   - The patient’s main concern and why they sought physiotherapy [N1-F1].

3. **History of present illness and urinary symptoms**  
   - Onset, duration, frequency, urgency, leakage pattern, triggers, and associated symptoms [N1-F1][N3-F3].

4. **Medical and obstetric history**  
   - Previous pregnancies, deliveries, episiotomy, perineal trauma, surgeries, infections, and other relevant medical history [N3-F3].

5. **Medications and supplements**  
   - Because these can affect pelvic floor function and treatment [N1-F1].

6. **Concurrent symptoms and functional limitations**  
   - Pain, sexual function, bowel function, core stability, and mobility [N1-F1][N3-F3].

7. **Pelvic floor examination findings**  
   - Type of examination method used, contraction strength, endurance, coordination, tightness, pain, and any abnormal movement [N1-F1][N2-F2].

8. **Differential diagnosis and red flags**  
   - Which symptoms or findings suggest other causes and require further investigation [N1-F1][N6-R1].

9. **Assessment of patient readiness for therapy**  
   - Whether the patient is a good candidate for physiotherapy and whether further medical evaluation is indicated [N1-F1].

10. **Plan of care and next steps**  
    - Proposed treatment, frequency of reassessment, and referrals [N1-F1][N3-F3].

### How to organize patient history, symptoms, and functional impact

The evidence supports organizing the patient’s history around impairment, disability, and participation restrictions using the ICF framework [N1-F1]. This means the template should capture:
- **Impairment**: structural, physiological, or anatomical issues related to the pelvic floor or urinary system [N1-F1].
- **Disability**: restriction or loss of ability to perform normal functions or activities [N1-F1].
- **Participation restrictions**: how the condition limits the patient’s role, mobility, or daily activities [N1-F1].

For symptoms, the template should capture not only the type and frequency of urinary leakage but also the context in which it occurs, such as stress, urgency, or functional incontinence [N3-F3]. The APTA guide also notes that physical therapists assess the muscles of the pelvis, hips, and lower back, coordination, strength, and flexibility, which supports including musculoskeletal and core-related symptoms in the history [N3-F3].

### How to include pelvic floor examination findings and differential considerations

The pelvic floor examination should be documented objectively and clinically. The evidence review indicates that digital palpation and perineometry are among the most commonly used procedures, and that objective assessment is important for accurate baseline and endpoint measurements [N2-F2]. The PERFECT scheme also provides a useful framework for documenting contraction, endurance, repetitions, and fast movement [N2-R2]. The assessment template should therefore include:
- Type of examination method used
- Contraction strength and pressure or Oxford-scale score
- Endurance and repetition capacity
- Coordination and movement pattern
- Any signs of tightness, weakness, or pain
- Any abnormal findings such as asymmetry, spasm, or lack of control [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R5]

For differential considerations, the evidence supports using a structured approach. The physiotherapy assessment paper emphasizes red flags that may indicate a need for medical consultation [N1-F1]. The StatPearls differential diagnosis aid also provides a mnemonic (DIAPPERS) for reversible causes of urinary incontinence, which can help organize differential thinking [N6-R1]. The NHS and AAFP sources also note that a pelvic examination is part of the diagnostic process, and that external gynecologic examination can detect atrophic vaginitis or vulvar irritation [N6-R2][N6-R3].

In practice, the template should document:
- Which symptoms or findings support a pelvic floor diagnosis
- Which findings raise concern for non-pelvic or other pelvic causes
- Whether further investigations are indicated [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3]

---

## 2. Recommended muscle strength assessment methods and typical measurements

Pelvic floor muscle strength assessment should be treated as a combination of objective and subjective methods because no single method is universally considered the “gold standard.” The evidence review explicitly states that multiple methods have been used, including clinical palpation, perineometer, electromyography, dynamometer, ultrasonography, magnetic resonance imaging, and vaginal cones, and that no one method can accurately calculate PFM strength alone [N2-F2]. A practical implication is that therapists should use the most clinically feasible method for the patient, with perineometry and ultrasonography highlighted as among the most commonly used methods in the literature [N2-F2].

### How to measure pelvic floor muscle strength

The evidence supports a structured measurement process that includes reproducibility and interpretation. The review notes that PFM strength assessment is a crucial part of clinical and technical discourse, and that a technique must be both objective and universal to provide precise baseline and endpoint measurements [N2-F2]. This means assessments should be standardized across sessions and practitioners where possible. The review also identifies digital palpation and perineometry as among the most often employed procedures [N2-F2], which is useful for documentation because it means therapists can record whether the chosen method is palpation, perineometry, or another objective test [N2-F2].

### What measurements are typically recorded

The evidence base suggests that assessment should cover contraction, endurance, and coordination. The PERFECT acronym in the search result provides a useful framework: P = power (pressure, a measure of strength using a manometric perineometer), E = endurance, R = repetitions, F = fast [N2-R2]. This indicates that therapists should routinely record strength under load or pressure, how long the muscle can sustain contraction, and the number or quality of repeated contractions. A separate source also notes that clinicians may use a modified Oxford scale in combination with vaginal palpation [N2-R5], which can be used to rate perceived strength on a scale from 1 to 5 or similar.

In practice, a standard record should therefore include:
- **Baseline contraction strength**: e.g., pressure reading or Oxford-scale score [N2-R2][N2-R5]
- **Endurance**: how many sustained contractions can be performed in sequence [N2-R2]
- **Coordination**: whether contractions are smooth, symmetrical, and appropriate [N2-F2][N2-R2]
- Any signs of weakness, tightness, or abnormal muscle behavior [N2-F2]

### How to interpret results in relation to clinical relevance and treatment planning

Interpretation should be tied to whether the findings support a diagnosis of pelvic floor dysfunction and guide treatment. The evidence review notes that PFM strength assessment is part of the clinical discourse on pelvic floor training and is essential for exercise prescription and successful treatment [N2-F2]. It also states that clinical palpation and perineometry are the most commonly used procedures, which implies that therapists should interpret these findings in the context of the patient’s symptoms and response to therapy [N2-F2].

In treatment planning, weak contraction or poor endurance suggests the need for strengthening exercises, while coordination problems or tightness may point to neuromuscular retraining or biofeedback [N2-F2][N2-R2]. The evidence from postpartum rehabilitation also supports the use of evidence-based treatment plans rooted in current research on postpartum pelvic floor rehab [N5-R4], which reinforces that assessment findings should directly inform the plan rather than be treated as standalone numbers.

### Reproducibility and interpretation caveats

The literature review explicitly cautions that no one method can accurately calculate PFM strength, and that combining methods tends to produce the best outcomes [N2-F2]. This means therapists should document whether multiple methods were used, which method was chosen, and whether findings were consistent across methods. The review also notes that correlation studies have shown variable agreement between digital palpation and perineometry, with some studies reporting moderate to significant correlation and others weaker correlation [N2-F2]. Therefore, interpretation should include a note on method limitations and whether results are within expected ranges for the patient’s condition.

## 3. Frequency of reassessment and plan of care recommendations

The evidence base supports a structured, evidence-based care plan for postpartum urinary incontinence, with reassessment and modification based on response to therapy. The APTA pelvic health guide states that physical therapists design treatment programs to improve pelvic floor muscle strength and help people gain control over the condition, and that treatment plans should be customized [N3-F3]. It also notes that physical therapists may refer patients to a doctor for urodynamic testing or other investigations if needed, which is useful for planning reassessment [N3-F3]. The postpartum pelvic floor therapy source adds that many moms start therapy within six weeks after delivery, but care is never too late, which supports a flexible but timely reassessment schedule [N5-R2].

### How often to reassess muscle strength and symptoms during therapy

The evidence does not provide a single fixed interval for reassessment, but the APTA guide emphasizes that the treatment program is tailored and that the physical therapist will perform a thorough exam and may refer for additional tests [N3-F3]. The physiotherapy assessment paper also notes that the assessment process is used to optimize patient selection and formulate a specific treatment plan, implying that reassessment should occur at intervals sufficient to monitor response and adjust the plan [N1-F1]. In practice, the most defensible approach is to reassess muscle strength and symptoms at regular intervals, such as 4–6 weeks after the initial evaluation, and then more frequently if the patient is responding poorly or if new symptoms emerge [N3-F3][N5-R2].

The physiotherapy assessment source also mentions severity calculation based on frequency counts for each response, which suggests that symptom frequency and severity should be tracked over time rather than assessed only once [N4-R5]. This supports the idea of using a diary or symptom tracker as part of the care plan [N1-F1][N4-R5].

### When to advance or modify the plan of care based on response

The evidence supports advancing or modifying the plan when there is a clear response to therapy. The postpartum pelvic floor therapy source states that treatment plans are designed to reduce or eliminate PFD symptoms and long-term complications, and that therapy can help patients feel strong and confident [N5-R3]. The APTA guide similarly states that the goal is to improve pelvic floor muscle function and reduce the need for pads, special underwear, and medicine [N3-F3]. If the patient shows improvement in contraction strength, endurance, coordination, and symptom frequency, the plan should be advanced; if there is little change or worsening, the plan should be modified [N3-F3][N5-R3].

The physiotherapy assessment paper also emphasizes that the assessment stage includes explicit decision-making about whether physiotherapy is indicated and what the treatment plan should be [N1-F1]. This implies that reassessment should trigger a decision point: if the patient is improving, advance the plan; if not, consider changing the intervention or investigating other causes [N1-F1][N3-F3].

### What evidence-based components should be included in the plan of care

A strong evidence-based plan should include the following components:
1. **Muscle-strengthening exercises**: the evidence supports strengthening the pelvic floor and improving awareness and movement [N3-F3].
2. **Biofeedback or manual facilitation**: although not explicitly detailed in the provided evidence, the assessment framework in the physiotherapy paper implies that objective assessment informs whether biofeedback or manual techniques are needed [N1-F1][N2-F2].
3. **Pelvic floor retraining**: the evidence base supports improving coordination and control [N3-F3].
4. **Education and lifestyle counseling**: the APTA guide states that physical therapists improve quality of life through patient education and prescribed movement, and the postpartum source mentions trauma-informed care and clear communication [N3-F3][N5-R4].
5. **Referral for investigations**: when the physical therapist identifies red flags or unclear pathology, referral for urodynamic testing or other investigations is appropriate [N3-F3][N1-F1].
6. **Progress monitoring**: tracking symptoms, frequency, and strength over time [N4-R5][N1-F1].

In short, the plan should be evidence-based, patient-centered, and dynamic: it should be reassessed regularly, advanced when the patient improves, and modified when the response is inadequate [N3-F3][N5-R2][N1-F1].

---

## 4. Differential diagnosis and clinical decision-making framework

The evidence supports a structured differential diagnosis approach for postpartum urinary incontinence, distinguishing pelvic floor dysfunction from other pelvic and non-pelvic causes. The physiotherapy assessment paper explicitly states that the initial management of urinary incontinence should be based on a medical diagnosis that may not always account for co-morbidities or functional limitations [N1-F1]. This means the therapist must consider both pelvic floor-related and non-pelvic contributors before deciding on physiotherapy as the primary intervention.

### How to distinguish postpartum urinary incontinence from other pelvic floor and non-pelvic causes

The evidence base suggests that postpartum urinary incontinence is often attributed to pelvic floor dysfunction, but it may also be caused by other pelvic structures or non-pelvic conditions. The APTA guide explains that urinary incontinence involves the muscles of the pelvic floor, but also notes that different types of incontinence may have different underlying mechanisms, including stress incontinence, urge incontinence, mixed incontinence, and functional incontinence [N3-F3]. The physiotherapy assessment paper similarly emphasizes that the assessment process investigates the nature of the underlying disorders and co-existing functional limitations [N1-F1].

Key differentiating features include:
- **Stress incontinence**: leakage with physical activity, coughing, laughing, or lifting; often linked to pelvic floor weakness or trauma [N3-F3].
- **Urge incontinence**: sudden, strong need to void with possible leakage before reaching the toilet; may reflect detrusor overactivity or poor coordination [N3-F3].
- **Mixed incontinence**: combination of stress and urge symptoms [N3-F3].
- **Functional incontinence**: caused by mobility, cognition, depression, or barriers to access, not directly by pelvic floor weakness [N3-F3].
- **Non-pelvic causes**: conditions such as infection, bladder outlet obstruction, diabetes, Parkinson disease, or neurological disorders [N6-R1][N6-R2].

The evidence also notes that the pelvic floor examination can help identify functional limitations and co-morbidities that affect outcomes [N1-F1]. This means the therapist should ask about fatigue, pain, mobility, cognition, and other factors that may limit participation or explain persistent symptoms [N1-F1][N3-F3].

### When to refer for urodynamic testing or other investigations

The evidence supports referral when the clinical picture is unclear or when the therapist identifies red flags. The physiotherapy assessment paper states that before starting the physiotherapy assessing process, the therapist should screen for pathological conditions that would require medical consultation and pay particular attention to red flags [N1-F1]. The APTA guide also notes that the physical therapist may refer the patient to a doctor for more tests, including urodynamic testing or imaging [N3-F3].

Urodynamic testing is explicitly described in the physiotherapy assessment paper as a gold standard for condition-specific diagnosis, though it is typically done in secondary care [N1-R2]. This makes it a useful investigation when the therapist is uncertain about the diagnosis, the patient has failed conservative management, or there are atypical symptoms such as unexplained leakage, frequent urination, or pain [N1-F1][N1-R2].

Other investigations may include:
- Pelvic examination to assess for atrophic vaginitis or vulvar irritation [N6-R2][N6-R3]
- Urinalysis or culture for infection [N6-R1]
- Imaging or MRI if structural abnormalities are suspected [N1-R2]

### How to document findings that support or refute a specific diagnosis

Documentation should clearly link findings to diagnostic possibilities. The evidence-based assessment framework recommends using the ICF model to distinguish impairment, disability, and participation restriction [N1-F1]. This means the therapist should document:
- Whether the patient’s symptoms are consistent with stress, urge, mixed, or functional incontinence
- Whether pelvic floor findings support weak contraction, poor endurance, or coordination
- Whether there are signs of tightness, pain, or abnormal movement that point to a different diagnosis
- Whether co-morbidities or functional limitations are present and may explain the symptoms [N1-F1][N3-F3]

The differential diagnosis aid (DIAPPERS) is useful for organizing reversible causes, including delirium, infection, constipation, medication use, pain, endocrine disease, and structural obstruction [N6-R1]. This can be used to document which reversible factors have been ruled in or out and what remains to be investigated [N6-R1].

---

## Final recommendation

For a standardized initial evaluation template, use the ICF-based structure outlined above: patient identification, history, symptoms, functional impact, pelvic floor examination findings, differential considerations, and plan of care [N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-R1]. For muscle strength assessment, use a combination of objective and subjective methods, recording contraction, endurance, coordination, and any abnormal findings, with interpretation tied to clinical relevance and treatment planning [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R5]. Reassess regularly, such as every 4–6 weeks, and advance or modify the plan based on response to therapy [N3-F3][N5-R2]. Referral for urodynamic testing or other investigations is appropriate when the clinical picture is unclear or when red flags are present [N1-F1][N3-F3][N1-R2].

This approach is consistent with the evidence from postpartum pelvic floor rehabilitation, pelvic floor muscle strength assessment, and urinary incontinence management guidelines [N3-F3][N5-R4][N2-F2].
